newsitem.title: USA: Hearing set for Monday on Staples-Office Depot deal.
newsitem.headline: Hearing set for Monday on Staples-Office Depot deal.

text.p: After months of manoeuvring, Staples Inc. and Office Depot Inc. go to court Monday to battle government charges that their merger will raise prices for copy paper, envelopes and a host of other items.

The five-member Federal Trade Commission voted this spring to challenge the $4 billion merger of the two office supply "superstore" chains and the companies responded by launching a costly court challenge to that decision.
The hearing, which is expected to last all week, follows months of wrangling between the government and the two big chains, which announced their proposed merger last fall.

Along the way, the FTC surprised many investors by voting twice to oppose the merger, even after the companies restructured the deal, agreeing to sell about 60 stores to OfficeMax Inc., a third big office supply chain.

Federal District Court Judge Thomas Hogan will hear from numerous witnesses -- including experts, customers, officers and suppliers -- followed by closing arguments next month and a ruling on whether to grant a preliminary injunction.

Essentially, the FTC argues that its studies -- and the stores' own price records -- show that in cities where Staples and Office Depot compete against each other, prices on office supplies are lower than in other places.
The superstores say they price against all kinds of competitors, such as Wal-Mart, but the FTC says the price records prove otherwise.

For example, the FTC said Office Depot advertised a box of copy paper for $24.99 in Leesburg, Fla., where there was no superstore competition, compared with $17.99 in Orlando, where there was superstore competition. It said envelopes were $4.79 vs. $2.79 and binders $2.99 vs. $1.72.
"We think we're right, we think we've got a strong case and we look forward to presenting our evidence in court," said William Baer, director of the FTC Bureau of Competition.
The two companies dismiss the claim and say they will prove it wrong.

"The FTC's evidence was fabricated out of whole cloth to support untested new theories," Don Kempf, lead attorney for the chains, said in an interview Friday. "It has been discredited by the people who buy and sell office supplies out in the real world instead of ivory towers."
That aggressive stance has marked the self-assurance of the chains, which took out full-page advertisements in major newspapers this year to make their case.

But outside observers have been unable to judge who is right, because lawyers for Staples and Office Depot argued successfully in court to keep pricing documents at the heart of the government's case secret.
Reuters, Dow Jones and Bloomberg news services all argued in court to no avail that the papers should be opened.
Whatever happens now, from the point of view of the FTC at least, the judge's ruling is merely a first step.

All Hogan needs to decide is whether there is reason to halt the merger for now. After that, a full-blown administrative trial, which could last months, will take place before an FTC administrative law judge.
The FTC says the administrative trial is the time to carefully consider all of the evidence.

But lawyers for Staples and Office Depot see it differently. They say that if they lose the first case and an injunction is granted, their clients will probably give up the effort to merge, rather than pursue the legal process further.
To them, the preliminary injunction hearing is virtually the trial, and they won the right to bring suppliers, customers and officers of the two chains to court.
The FTC dismisses such moves as an effort to divert attention from the main case, which it says is based on the papers that show what has happened to prices.
In the meantime, three states have opened their own investigations of the case.
Staples stock rose 75 cents to $22.377 on Nasdaq and Office Depot rose 50 cents to $16.25 on the New York Stock Exchange.
